title: Admin Culture Picker and the Content-Language Header

chapters.title: Admin Culture Picker and the Content-Language Header
chapters.subtitle: Choose the language of the admin, and name the language of the responses

steps.text: A site can be published in one language while its editors prefer to work in another. The Localization module has two small features around language: the Admin Culture Picker and the Content Language Header. Let's see what each one does.
A culture is a language, with a region when it has one, such as English for the United States. A site lists the cultures it supports in its settings.

The Admin Culture Picker is a drop-down in the admin top bar. It lists the supported cultures of the site. The admin follows your choice: the labels that have a translation, and the text direction of a language written right to left.
The Content Language Header has no screen and no settings. When it is enabled, the responses of the site carry a header that names their language.

The picker needs the Localization feature and at least two supported cultures. Its labels change where the site has translations for the chosen culture, which PO files provide. A separate video covers installing them.
Both features are on the Features page, under Tools. They belong to the Internationalization category, and the search box finds them by name. Let's search for Admin Culture Picker.
Its row lists Localization as a dependency. Orchard Core enables a dependency together with the feature, so let's click Enable. A message confirms that the feature was enabled.
Let's search for Content Language Header, and enable it the same way. Its row lists the same dependency, Localization.
Searching for Localization shows that this feature is enabled as well, along with the two features we enabled.

chapters.title: Supported cultures
chapters.subtitle: A second culture makes the picker appear

steps.text: Localization adds a Cultures page to the admin menu, under Settings, Localization. The site supports a single culture, so the top bar shows no culture picker.
Let's choose French in the list, click Add culture, and Save. A separate video covers the Cultures page in detail.
A message says the site restarted for the settings to take effect. When the page loads again, the top bar shows a drop-down with the name of the current culture.

chapters.title: Choose the admin culture
chapters.subtitle: Admin pages only, one choice per browser

steps.text: Let's open the drop-down. It lists the other supported cultures, each under its own name, and leaves out the current one.
Let's choose français. The page reloads, and the menu and the labels that have a French translation appear in French.
A label without a French translation stays in English, because the picker changes the culture, not the translations.
Let's visit the site with the Visit Site icon. The front end does not follow the choice, because the choice applies to the admin pages only.
Let's return to the admin. The pages stay in French, because the choice is stored in a cookie of this browser.
To switch back, let's open the drop-down and choose English (United States). The cookie changes no setting of the site, and another browser has its own choice.

chapters.title: The Content Language Header
chapters.subtitle: A header on the responses of the site

steps.text: The header describes the language intended for the audience. Its value is the culture the site uses to render the response, the same culture that selects the translations.
A page in English carries the English culture. In the admin, the header follows the picker, so a page shown in français carries the French culture.

chapters.title: Admin Culture Picker and the Content-Language Header
chapters.subtitle: docs.orchardcore.net

steps.text: The Admin Culture Picker sets the language of the admin for your browser, and the Content Language Header names the language of the responses of the site. Thanks for watching.
